summary:
Magadan Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and every source consulted treats that framework as applying uniformly across the country. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out that framework, and none of its findings are specific to Magadan Oblast. A visitor to Magadan Oblast faces the same legal exposure as a visitor to Moscow or Vladivostok.

Consensual same-sex activity is not itself a criminal offence in Russia, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. The 2023 law prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year. The Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023. The expanded propaganda statutes criminalise any public expression, including anything explicitly justifying gender transition.

The practical consequence for a transgender visitor is that no document can be brought into alignment with their gender presentation. Any police stop, hotel registration, bank or transport identity check reads as a mismatch between presentation and papers. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

Enforcement is documented at national scale. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. The same organisation documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The UK Home Office note records at least 139 individuals affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024.

Volume has risen alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

The enforcement figures available are national totals. Neither Human Rights Watch nor the UK Home Office note breaks its counts down by federal subject, so the share attributable to Magadan Oblast cannot be read from these sources.
localsOnly:
Residents of Magadan Oblast live under the same bans as the rest of Russia: same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. Consensual same-sex activity is not a criminal offence.

Administrative liability under article 20.3 covers displaying banned LGBT symbols, and the UK Home Office note records 81 people found guilty in 98 such cases since January 2024, mostly for social media posts. "Gay propaganda" fines for individuals reach 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention, and extremism-related charges carry up to 12 years in prison. At least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024.

The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement action, raids, extremism charges or convictions originating in Magadan Oblast itself. Whether oblast-level police have conducted venue raids or applied the extremist designation locally is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The conversion-therapy case documented by BBC Russian (27 July 2024) took place near Novosibirsk, not in Magadan Oblast; it is cited as evidence of documented physical coercion against transgender people in Russia rather than as a local finding.

The UK Home Office note is version 2.0, June 2025, with its page updated 12 August 2026. Whether its counts have been refreshed since publication is not stated in the material available.
